title: India's Aditya-L1 and Europe's Proba-3 Decode Solar Eruptions Together for First Time
excerpt: Joint observations from ISRO's VELC and ESA's ASPIICS coronagraphs measured the mass, density and energy of two coronal mass ejections close to the Sun, in a first published analysis in Astronomy & Astrophysics.
body:
• Scientists have jointly analysed the same solar eruptions using India's Aditya-L1 and Europe's Proba-3 for the first time, with results published in Astronomy & Astrophysics.
  • Only two coronal mass ejections, on 14 and 16 September 2025, were caught by both spacecraft between July and December 2025.
  • The two eruptions behaved very differently — one travelled at about 645 km/s, the other at 145 km/s — yet independent measurements from the two instruments agreed closely.
  • Better measurements close to the Sun should improve understanding of eruptions that, when aimed at Earth, can disturb satellites, navigation and power systems.

India's Aditya-L1 solar observatory and the European Space Agency's Proba-3 mission have produced their first joint study of solar eruptions, according to ISRO. Researchers at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics in Bengaluru combined data from the two spacecraft to measure the mass, density and energy of coronal mass ejections very close to the Sun, in a paper published in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

Two instruments, one eruption

Aditya-L1, India's first dedicated solar mission, was launched on 2 September 2023 and entered a halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point on 6 January 2024, giving it an uninterrupted view of the Sun. Its Visible Emission Line Coronagraph, known as VELC, was developed by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics with ISRO and records spectroscopic observations of the corona from 1.05 to 1.5 solar radii.

Proba-3 took a different approach. Launched from Sriharikota on 5 December 2024, it is the world's first precision formation-flying mission: two spacecraft fly about 150 metres apart, with one casting a shadow on the other to create an artificial solar eclipse in space. Its ASPIICS coronagraph images the corona from about 1.1 to 3 solar radii. Because VELC measures spectra while ASPIICS takes images, the pair can cross-check the same event in two independent ways.

What the joint observations found

The overlap proved rare. From July to December 2025, only two eruptions — on 14 and 16 September — were recorded simultaneously by both instruments, and in both cases VELC caught the eruptions at an early stage. The study, led by Anjali Agarwal and colleagues, found sharply different behaviour in the two events.

The 14 September eruption was fast, at about 645 km/s, and its thermal energy was only about 1% of the total, indicating limited heating of the ejected plasma. The 16 September eruption moved far more slowly, at 145 km/s, expanded more strongly, and saw its thermal energy rise until it matched its kinetic energy. In both events, magnetic energy was comparable to or greater than kinetic energy. Crucially, mass and thermal-energy estimates from the two instruments agreed well despite relying on different methods and assumptions.

Why measurements near the Sun matter

Coronal mass ejections hurl huge amounts of magnetised plasma into space. When one is directed at Earth, it can disturb the near-Earth environment, with consequences for satellites and communications. Measuring an eruption near its birthplace is difficult, however, and earlier coronagraphs only partly succeeded in tracking faint eruptions in the inner corona, leaving open how their energy is divided between motion, heat and magnetism.

The joint work addresses that gap. VELC's spectroscopy provides information on gas at about two million degrees, yielding independent estimates of density and thermal energy, while ASPIICS images give the shape, dynamics and mass. Together they offer a more complete, cross-checked picture of how an eruption begins.

What comes next

ISRO said the results demonstrate the potential of coordinated observations to constrain the properties of eruptions in the inner corona. The study involved researchers from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics alongside European and American solar physicists, extending a collaboration that also brought Proba-3 to orbit on an Indian launcher. For readers in the diaspora working in aerospace and research, it is a concrete example of an Indian mission contributing data that European teams now rely on as well.
